"""Read INI configuration files.

The text is read line by line:

- Blank lines, and lines whose first non-space character is ``#`` or ``;``,
  are ignored, and end any value being continued.
- ``[name]`` (surrounding whitespace allowed) starts a section. Section
  names are stripped and case-sensitive. A section that appears again
  continues the earlier one.
- ``key = value`` or ``key: value`` sets a key in the current section,
  splitting at the first ``=`` or ``:``, whichever comes first. Keys are
  stripped and lowercased, values stripped; a key appearing again in a
  section replaces the earlier value.
- A line starting with whitespace, directly after a key line or another
  continuation line, continues that key's value: its stripped text is
  appended after a ``\\n``. Any other line is read as above after
  stripping it.

A key before any section, a line that is none of the above, or an empty
key raises ``ParseError`` with the 1-based line number.

After the whole text is read, values are interpolated: ``${key}`` is
replaced with the value of ``key`` in the same section, ``${section:key}``
with the value from another section, and ``$$`` with a literal ``$``
(which is not interpolated further); any other ``$`` is left as it is.
Interpolation is recursive: referenced values are interpolated too. A
reference to a missing key or section, or a cycle, raises
``InterpolationError``. Keys inside references are lowercased like other
keys.

``parse`` returns a dict of section names to dicts of keys to values, with
sections and keys in the order they first appear.
"""

class ParseError(ValueError):
    def __init__(self, lineno: int, message: str):
        super().__init__(f"line {lineno}: {message}")
        self.lineno = lineno


class InterpolationError(ValueError):
    pass


def parse(text: str) -> dict[str, dict[str, str]]:
    """Parse INI text."""
    raise NotImplementedError

"""Read INI configuration files.

The text is read line by line:

- Blank lines, and lines whose first non-space character is ``#`` or ``;``,
  are ignored, and end any value being continued.
- ``[name]`` (surrounding whitespace allowed) starts a section. Section
  names are stripped and case-sensitive. A section that appears again
  continues the earlier one.
- ``key = value`` or ``key: value`` sets a key in the current section,
  splitting at the first ``=`` or ``:``, whichever comes first. Keys are
  stripped and lowercased, values stripped; a key appearing again in a
  section replaces the earlier value.
- A line starting with whitespace, directly after a key line or another
  continuation line, continues that key's value: its stripped text is
  appended after a ``\\n``. Any other line is read as above after
  stripping it.

A key before any section, a line that is none of the above, or an empty
key raises ``ParseError`` with the 1-based line number.

After the whole text is read, values are interpolated: ``${key}`` is
replaced with the value of ``key`` in the same section, ``${section:key}``
with the value from another section, and ``$$`` with a literal ``$``
(which is not interpolated further); any other ``$`` is left as it is.
Interpolation is recursive: referenced values are interpolated too. A
reference to a missing key or section, or a cycle, raises
``InterpolationError``. Keys inside references are lowercased like other
keys.

``parse`` returns a dict of section names to dicts of keys to values, with
sections and keys in the order they first appear.
"""

from __future__ import annotations


class ParseError(ValueError):
    def __init__(self, lineno: int, message: str):
        super().__init__(f"line {lineno}: {message}")
        self.lineno = lineno


class InterpolationError(ValueError):
    pass


def parse(text: str) -> dict[str, dict[str, str]]:
    """Parse INI text."""

"""Semantic version parsing, comparison, and range matching.

Versions follow Semantic Versioning 2.0.0: ``MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH``, then an
optional pre-release (``-`` followed by dot-separated identifiers) and an
optional build (``+`` followed by dot-separated identifiers). Identifiers
are non-empty and made of ASCII letters, digits, and hyphens. Numeric parts
(MAJOR, MINOR, PATCH, and all-digit pre-release identifiers) must not have
leading zeros. Anything else is invalid and raises ``ValueError``.

Precedence (``compare``) follows the SemVer 2.0.0 rules: compare MAJOR,
MINOR, and PATCH numerically; a version with a pre-release is lower than
the same version without one; pre-release identifiers are compared left to
right, all-digit ones numerically and the rest in ASCII order, with
all-digit identifiers lower than the rest, and a shorter list lower when
all its identifiers equal the start of a longer one. Build metadata is
ignored.

Ranges (``satisfies``) are one or more comparator sets joined by ``||``; a
version satisfies the range if it satisfies any set. A set is one or more
comparators separated by whitespace, all of which must hold. A comparator
is a full version optionally prefixed by an operator:

- ``=`` (or no operator), ``>``, ``>=``, ``<``, ``<=``: by precedence.
- ``^X.Y.Z``: at least ``X.Y.Z`` and below the next version that changes
  the leftmost non-zero part, i.e. ``^1.2.3`` is ``>=1.2.3 <2.0.0``,
  ``^0.2.3`` is ``>=0.2.3 <0.3.0``, and ``^0.0.3`` is ``>=0.0.3 <0.0.4``.
- ``~X.Y.Z``: at least ``X.Y.Z`` and below ``X.(Y+1).0``.

A version with a pre-release satisfies a set only if some comparator in
that set has a pre-release on the same MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH (so
``1.2.3-beta.2`` satisfies ``>=1.2.3-beta.1`` but not ``>=1.0.0``).
Invalid ranges raise ``ValueError``.
"""

_NUMBER = r"(?:0|[1-9][0-9]*)"
_IDENTS = r"[0-9A-Za-z-]+(?:\.[0-9A-Za-z-]+)*"
_VERSION_RE = re.compile(
    rf"({_NUMBER})\.({_NUMBER})\.({_NUMBER})(?:-({_IDENTS}))?(?:\+({_IDENTS}))?"
)
_DIGITS_RE = re.compile(r"[0-9]+")
_COMPARATOR_RE = re.compile(r"(>=|<=|>|<|=|\^|~)?(.*)", re.DOTALL)

class Version:
    major: int
    minor: int
    patch: int
    prerelease: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    build: tuple[str, ...] = ()

    def __str__(self) -> str:
        """The version in canonical form, e.g. ``1.2.3-rc.1+build.5``."""
        text = f"{self.major}.{self.minor}.{self.patch}"
        if self.prerelease:
            text += "-" + ".".join(self.prerelease)
        if self.build:
            text += "+" + ".".join(self.build)
        return text

    """Parse a version string."""
    match = _VERSION_RE.fullmatch(text)

        raise ValueError(f"invalid version: {text!r}")
    major, minor, patch, prerelease, build = match.groups()
    prerelease_ids = tuple(prerelease.split(".")) if prerelease else ()

- **`satisfies`** turns each comparator into lower and upper bounds (`^` and `~` included) and applies the pre-release rule to each set separately. It reads the whole range before evaluating anything, so an invalid range always raises `ValueError`, even if an earlier set would already match.
- I added four small private helpers: `_as_version`, `_precedence_key`, `_parse_comparator` and `_holds`.

**Places where the spec was unclear, and what I chose:**
1. **`^0.0.0`**: there is no non-zero part, so I extended the `0.0.x` rule and made it `>=0.0.0 <0.0.1`.
2. **Space between operator and version** (`>= 1.2.3`): the spec says comparators are separated by whitespace, so this is a lone `>=` followed by `1.2.3`, and it raises `ValueError`.

6. **`Version` objects passed in directly** are used as they are, without re-validating them.

`next_run` is implemented in `/private/tmp/tmpn15c963i/pete/projects/devkit/devkit/cron.py` and passes all my checks. No other repo files were touched.

**How it works**
- **Parsing:** each field is turned into a set of allowed values by a small regex plus `_value` and `_parse_field` helpers.
  - Names are accepted in any case, including in ranges (`mon-FRI`). Month names only work in the month field and day names only in the day-of-week field.
  - `N/S` runs from N to the end of the field's range, and day-of-week 7 becomes 0.
  - These all raise `ValueError`: values out of range, `A > B` ranges, a step of 0, empty items like `1,,2`, malformed items like `*-5`, `+5`, `-1`, `1-2-3`, `*/5/2` or non-ASCII digits, and any field count other than five.
- **Day rule:** a day matches if it matches day-of-month or day-of-week when both fields are restricted, and must match both otherwise.
- **Search:** it starts at `after` with seconds dropped, plus one minute. It skips whole months that don't match and steps day by day through the rest (at most about 1,830 days). On the first matching day it picks the hour and minute directly from the sorted lists, so it never loops over minutes. A run that hasn't finished in about 0.1 ms means a five-year search ending in `ValueError`; 200 calls took 0.016 s.

**Spec ambiguities and what I chose**
1. **"Exactly `*`":** I read this literally, so `*/1` or `*/2` counts as restricted and turns on the either-day rule. Real Vixie cron treats any field starting with `*` as unrestricted, so this differs from it on purpose.
2. **The five-year limit:** a match counts if it is at or before `after` plus five calendar years. If `after` is Feb 29, the limit is Feb 28 five years later. As a side effect, `0 0 29 2 *` raises from 2097 onward, because there is no Feb 29 in 2100 and the next one is 2104.
3. **Day-of-week ranges:** the range is 0-7, so `5-7` means Fri, Sat, Sun and `1/3` means Mon, Thu, Sun.

**What I verified**
I used a throwaway script at `/private/tmp/tmpn15c963i/tmp/cron_check.py`. `/tmp` isn't writable from the sandbox, so I used the session's temp directory, which is outside the repo.
- **Hand-written cases:** every example in the docstring, Sunday as both 0 and 7, the either-day rule versus the both-must-match rule, crossing year and month ends, inputs that already land exactly on a minute or carry seconds and microseconds, extra whitespace, about 28 invalid expressions, `0 0 30 2 *` and the 2097 Feb 29 case.
- **Brute-force comparison:** 1,500 random expressions with random `after` times, each checked against a minute-by-minute search, all agreeing. That search reuses my parser, so it only checks the search logic; the parsing is covered by the hand-written cases.

I also split one regex line to keep it under 80 characters, to match the rest of the file.
